The demo's opening move. Tier 1 means the approval flow adds no prompt, NOT that the call is allowed: the refusal is a hard one from the skill profile (credentials.allow, http.post_paths) and EgressClient, neither of which is this gate. A corpus line asserting refused here would be asserting it of the wrong layer.
Same: the egress allowlist refuses a non-listed host before the vault is touched, and records a refusal rather than a prompt.
A model-set Authorization header is refused inside the http_request tool, again below this gate.
Scheme validation is the tool's, not the tier gate's.
A credential-shaped absolute path is not special to the tier gate. cap-std opens the workspace with RESOLVE_BENEATH, so the escape is refused at the syscall layer, not here.
Traversal is likewise a cap-std refusal, not a tier decision.
Workspace writes are Tier 1 and confined by the same capability handle. Persistence outside the workspace is refused there.
Listing / is a confinement question, not a tier one.

why: Writing memory is the workspace write tier.
Reading another channel's entries crosses a trust zone. The key carries the source channel, so approving one channel approves no other.
A missing channel yields an empty key that no entry carries, so it denies rather than widening.
Same for an explicit empty string.
A wildcard is a literal channel name here, not a glob. It matches no channel and is keyed as itself.
Another account's conversation history. Keyed per source archive.
A missing source yields a key no archive carries.
A search scoped to one archive.
An unscoped search sweeps every archive and takes a key of its own, so approving one archive can never be mistaken for approving the sweep.
A whitespace-only source is the unscoped form, not an archive named three spaces.
Operator-chosen server names can contain underscores, so the prefix is not splittable. The whole name is the key, which is why an ambiguous split cannot widen a grant.
